title: Extreme Heat Is a Jobs Crisis—South Asia’s Cities Can’t Afford to Wait.
gist: The World Bank's South Asia VP argues extreme heat has become a labor-market and growth problem, not just a climate one: it already destroys the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs a year in South Asia and could cut regional GDP by nearly 7 percent by 2050 — the steepest projected loss of any developing region. The remedy proposed is heat-resilient urban infrastructure, institutionalized heat governance, and mobilized private capital into efficient cooling, buildings and energy systems.

themes.theme: Heat as a measurable macro drag

insights.claim: Extreme heat already subtracts the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs annually in South Asia as businesses face power, transport and operational disruption and workers slow, stop or fall ill.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Quantifies heat as an ongoing productivity tax already embedded in South Asian output, not a future risk to be discounted.
insights.quote: extreme heat already subtracts the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs annually

insights.claim: Without adaptation, rising temperatures could reduce South Asia's GDP by nearly 7 percent by 2050, the steepest projected loss of any developing region, cutting investment, government revenues and long-term competitiveness.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A 7% GDP haircut concentrated in one region reprices sovereign growth trajectories and fiscal capacity across South Asian credits.
insights.quote: rising temperatures could reduce South Asia's GDP by nearly 7 percent by 2050 - the steepest projected loss of any developing region
insights.locator: Without adaptation, rising temperatures could reduce

insights.claim: The number of South Asians facing a month or more each year of dangerous heat stress is projected to quadruple by 2070, from 120 million today to 520 million.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A 400 million person increase in populations requiring active cooling defines the long-run demand curve for cooling equipment and power capacity.
insights.locator: The number of South Asians facing a month or more each year

insights.claim: South Asia must create jobs for roughly 280 million new working-age people by 2050, with cities at the center of that effort just as those cities become least habitable.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The demographic dividend and the heat threat land on the same urban geography — the collision is the core investment case for adaptation spend.
insights.quote: The region needs to create jobs for about 280 million new working-age people by 2050.
insights.locator: Rekhaben's story is becoming increasingly common

insights.claim: Unlike floods or storms, heat leaves few visible signs of destruction, which causes its enormous economic costs to be systematically under-recognized.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Absence of visible damage means heat risk is underpriced in insurance, catastrophe modeling and infrastructure planning relative to flood and storm risk.
insights.quote: Unlike floods or storms, heat leaves few visible signs of destruction, yet its economic costs are enormous.

insights.claim: Heat-related deaths are typically recorded as cardiac or renal failure, so a five-day heatwave associated with some 30,000 excess deaths can pass unrecorded as a heat event.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Official mortality data understates heat impact by orders of magnitude, so excess-death studies rather than cause-coded statistics should drive risk models.
insights.quote: a five-day heatwave associated with some 30,000 excess deaths can pass unrecorded as a heat event
insights.locator: Much of the human cost does not appear in official statistics

insights.claim: Climate change, rapid urbanization and the urban heat-island effect are compounding to make South Asian cities hotter for longer than historical heat patterns.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Urban heat is partly self-inflicted through built form, meaning city-level design choices are a controllable variable independent of global emissions paths.
insights.locator: Heat has always been part of South Asian life

insights.claim: A heatwave can cause informal workers to lose 40 percent of their earnings while simultaneously raising their costs for water, cooling and healthcare.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A simultaneous income shock and cost shock on the same households implies heat events drive consumption collapse and microfinance stress in affected cities.
insights.quote: A heatwave can cause informal workers to lose 40 percent of their earnings while also raising costs for water, cooling, and healthcare.
insights.locator: The poor bear the greatest burden

insights.claim: Informal workers cannot opt out of heat exposure because daily earnings fund daily consumption, as illustrated by an Ahmedabad vegetable vendor who required IV drips and injections after 2025 heat yet could not stay home.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Behavioral adaptation is not available to the most exposed workers, so only infrastructure and income-support interventions actually change outcomes.
insights.locator: Extreme heat in 2025 left Rekhaben so weak

insights.claim: Early-warning systems generate an estimated $50 in benefits for every $1 invested.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A 50:1 benefit-cost ratio makes early warning the highest-return line item in the adaptation stack and the most likely to attract concessional financing first.
insights.quote: Early-warning systems generate an estimated $50 in benefits for every $1 invested.
insights.locator: Strengthening the institutions, rules, and planning

insights.claim: Ahmedabad's heat action plan has cut peak-heat mortality by 47 percent.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A near-halving of mortality from a municipal planning intervention is a replicable template that lowers the political cost of heat adaptation spending.
insights.quote: Ahmedabad’s heat action plan has cut peak-heat mortality by 47 percent.

insights.claim: Tamil Nadu's passive cool-roof initiative has cut indoor temperatures in government buildings by 4 to 5 degrees Celsius and is being expanded to schools.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Low-cost passive design delivering 4-5C indoor reduction competes directly with active cooling capex and suppresses future electricity demand growth.

insights.claim: Bihar, Tamil Nadu and Madhya Pradesh have recognized extreme heat as a recurring disaster risk requiring year-round attention, and India's Sixteenth Finance Commission has recommended extending that recognition nationally.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Formal disaster-risk classification unlocks dedicated fiscal transfers — a national designation would create a new recurring public procurement stream for cooling and resilience.
insights.locator: Three Indian states - Bihar, Tamil Nadu, and Madhya Pradesh

insights.claim: Cities globally are adjusting outdoor working hours during heat alerts, mandating rest and water at worksites, and extending income support to the poor when work becomes unsafe.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Mandated work-hour restrictions are a direct margin hit for construction, logistics and outdoor-labor-intensive businesses in hot geographies.
insights.locator: Cities around the world are adjusting outdoor working hours

insights.claim: Heat resilience must be embedded in everyday governance rather than treated as seasonal emergency response.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The shift from emergency to permanent budget line is what converts adaptation from episodic relief spending into a durable procurement market.
insights.locator: Strengthening the institutions, rules, and planning

themes.theme: Private capital and the cooling supply chain

insights.claim: Investing in resilient cooling supply chains, domestic manufacturing capability and next-generation technologies can make efficient cooling more affordable while strengthening energy security, creating jobs and reducing emissions.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Frames cooling as an industrial-policy opportunity, pointing to localized HVAC and refrigerant manufacturing build-outs in India and the region.
insights.locator: Mobilizing private investment to expand efficient cooling

insights.claim: Governments can suppress future cooling demand by integrating passive cooling principles into affordable housing and housing-for-all programs so today's construction remains comfortable in a hotter climate.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Building-code changes on mass housing programs are the cheapest lever on long-run peak power demand — watch for code revisions as a leading indicator for utilities.
insights.locator: Governments can also reduce future cooling demand

insights.claim: Decisions made over the next decade will determine whether South Asia's cities remain engines of opportunity or become constrained by extreme heat, because the buildings and infrastructure built today lock in tomorrow's productivity.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Capital-stock lock-in means adaptation delayed is adaptation forgone; the window for cheap retrofit-avoidance is roughly one decade.
insights.quote: The buildings, infrastructure, institutions, and industries constructed today will shape the region’s productivity and competitiveness tomorrow.
insights.locator: Decisions made over the next decade

insights.claim: Managing extreme heat has ceased to be only a climate imperative and is now central to South Asia's jobs and growth agenda.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Reclassifying heat from environment to growth policy moves it into finance-ministry budgets rather than environment-ministry ones, changing the funding scale entirely.
insights.quote: Managing extreme heat is no longer just a climate imperative. It has become central to South Asia's jobs and growth agenda.
insights.locator: A new World Bank report, A Livable Future
